ready2_open_rewrite.final_cot: Image description: In the diagram there is an equilateral triangle with a horizontal base. A square is placed on the right-side part of the triangle's base; the bottom side of the square coincides with the triangle's base, the lower right corner of the square is exactly the right endpoint of the triangle, and the upper left corner of the square falls on the left slanted side of the triangle. Reasoning: The square's perimeter is 4, so the side length of the square is 1. Let the side length of the equilateral triangle be s, then the triangle's base length is s. The square's bottom side occupies length 1 on the right side of the triangle's base, so the small base segment from the square's left side to the triangle's left endpoint has length s - 1. Since the left side of the equilateral triangle forms 60° with the base, in the right triangle formed by this small base segment and the square's left side, the height is 1 and the base is s - 1, so tan 60° = 1/(s - 1). Because tan 60° = √3, √3 = 1/(s - 1), giving s - 1 = 1/√3 = √3/3. Therefore s = 1 + √3/3. The perimeter of the equilateral triangle is 3s = 3(1 + √3/3) = 3 + √3.

method.method_draft: Read the diagram as an equilateral triangle with a horizontal base; the square sits on the right part of the base, its lower-right corner is the triangle’s right base vertex, and its upper-left corner lies on the triangle’s left slanted side. From the text, the square perimeter is 4, so each square side is 1. Let the equilateral triangle side length be s. Then the square’s bottom side contributes length 1 along the triangle base, leaving a small left base segment of length s-1. Because the left side of an equilateral triangle makes a 60° angle with the base, the small right triangle formed by this left base segment and the square’s left side has height 1 and angle 60°, so tan 60° = 1/(s-1). Thus s-1=1/√3=√3/3, so s=1+√3/3. The triangle perimeter is 3s=3+√3.
